entries.definition: A US pharmacy category that compounds medicines for individual patients based on a prescription.
A US outsourcing facility category that compounds drugs in bulk, often for clinics, under stricter manufacturing rules.
A test that measures how far a person can walk in six minutes, used to gauge exercise capacity.
95% confidence interval, a range that likely contains the true value of a measured result.
Hemoglobin A1C, a blood test showing average blood sugar over about the past three months.
Adeno-associated virus, a small harmless virus often used to carry genes into cells in gene therapy.
The space inside the belly that holds organs such as the stomach, liver and intestines.
Swelling or bloating of the belly.
Fat stored around the midsection, including fat deep around the organs.
A pocket of pus that forms in tissue as a result of infection.
The process by which a substance moves from where it is given into the bloodstream.
How likely a substance is to be misused or to lead to addiction.
A US FDA pathway that approves a drug earlier based on a surrogate result, with later studies needed to confirm benefit.
The thick tendon at the back of the ankle that connects the calf muscles to the heel bone.
A condition in which the blood or body fluids contain too much acid.
Anterior cruciate ligament, a key ligament that stabilizes the knee.
Surgery that replaces a torn anterior cruciate ligament in the knee with a graft.
Severe weight gain caused by damage to the hypothalamus, the brain region that helps control hunger and energy use.
A condition in which the body makes too much growth hormone in adults, causing enlarged hands, feet and facial features.
A protein that forms thin filaments inside cells and works with myosin to make muscles contract.
A signaling protein that regulates muscle growth, reproduction and other processes, and is blocked by follistatin.
A sudden loss of brain function caused by a blocked blood vessel cutting off blood flow to part of the brain.
A sudden drop in kidney function that can develop over hours or days.
Sudden inflammation of the pancreas, often causing severe upper abdominal pain.
Having a fatty acid chain attached, a change that can help a peptide last longer in the body.
A treatment given in addition to a treatment a person is already taking.
A small mass of tissue behind the nose and throat that helps fight infection.
An enzyme that makes cyclic AMP, a molecule cells use to relay signals from hormone receptors.
Fat cells, which store energy as fat.
The amount of body fat a person carries.
A treatment used alongside a main treatment to support it.
A condition in which the adrenal glands do not make enough of certain hormones such as cortisol.
A receptor on cells that responds to adrenaline and noradrenaline, affecting heart rate and blood pressure.
A hormone made in the pituitary gland that tells the adrenal glands to release cortisol.
Any unwanted effect that occurs during or after a treatment, whether or not the treatment caused it.
A panel of outside experts that reviews evidence and advises a regulator such as the FDA.
Web links that pay the site owner a commission when a visitor buys through them.
How strongly a molecule binds to its target, such as a receptor.
Declining sex hormone production, especially testosterone, that occurs with aging.
The clumping together of molecules such as peptides into larger masses.
Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, the advanced stage of HIV infection in which the immune system is badly weakened.
A family of enzymes that relay signals inside cells and help control cell growth and survival.
The most common protein in blood plasma, which helps carry substances through the body.
A small pad soaked in rubbing alcohol used to clean a vial stopper or skin before injection.
A condition in which a person cannot control or stop drinking despite harm.
Death from any cause, used as an outcome measure in studies.
An immune system response to a substance that is usually harmless, ranging from mild rash to severe reactions.
Acting at a site on a receptor or enzyme other than the main binding site, changing how it works.
A rare inherited disorder causing vision and hearing loss, obesity and insulin resistance.
Alanine aminotransferase, a liver enzyme measured in blood, with higher levels suggesting liver irritation.
A progressive brain disease that causes memory loss and declining thinking skills.
Recording a measure such as blood pressure over a full day while a person goes about normal activities.
The absence of menstrual periods.
The order of amino acids that make up a peptide or protein.
AMP-activated protein kinase, an enzyme that acts as a cell energy sensor and helps regulate metabolism.
A small sealed glass container holding a single dose of liquid medicine.
An almond-shaped brain region involved in processing emotions such as fear.
A hormone made with insulin in the pancreas that slows stomach emptying and promotes fullness.
A sticky clump of misfolded protein that builds up between brain cells in Alzheimer's disease.
A group of diseases in which abnormal protein builds up in organs and tissues.
Promoting the building of tissue, especially muscle.
A compound with a structure modified from a natural molecule, often to change how long it lasts or how strongly it acts.
A sudden, severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction.
A type of hormone that promotes male sex characteristics, such as testosterone.
A protein in cells that binds androgens such as testosterone and carries out their effects.
A tumor whose growth is driven by androgens such as testosterone.
Based on personal accounts or isolated cases rather than controlled studies.
A loss of feeling or awareness produced by drugs, used to prevent pain during surgery.
Swelling in the deeper layers of skin, often around the face, lips or throat, usually from an allergic reaction.
A hormone that narrows blood vessels and raises blood pressure.
An animal used in research to study a disease or treatment before human testing.
An eating disorder marked by intense fear of weight gain and severely restricted eating.
A substance that blocks a receptor or stops the action of another substance.
Relieving weakness and fatigue.
Rules and testing that aim to stop banned performance-enhancing substances in sport.
Reducing inflammation.
Proteins made by the immune system that attach to specific targets such as germs or foreign molecules.
A drug used to treat depression.
Reducing the amount of urine the body makes.
A drug that treats infections caused by fungi.
A drug that lowers high blood pressure.
A substance that kills microorganisms such as bacteria or mold, or stops them from growing.
A short protein fragment that kills or stops the growth of bacteria, fungi or viruses.
A substance that protects cells from damage caused by unstable molecules called free radicals.
A drug that slows bone breakdown.
A drug used to ease anxiety.
A quick score of a newborn's health, taken one and five minutes after birth.
Active pharmaceutical ingredient, the part of a drug that produces its intended effect.
Amyloid precursor protein, the protein from which the amyloid fragments in Alzheimer's disease are cut.
A drug or substance that reduces the desire to eat.
A drug that a regulator such as the FDA has authorized for sale for specific uses.
A solution in which the substance is dissolved in water.
An amino acid, one of the building blocks of proteins.
An enzyme that converts testosterone into estrogen.
A problem with the rate or rhythm of the heartbeat.
Joint pain.
Done through small cuts using a tiny camera to see inside a joint.
Used only when a situation calls for it rather than on a fixed schedule.
Groups of participants given progressively higher doses in sequence to test safety.
Describes a study design in which successive groups of participants receive higher and higher doses to see how each dose is tolerated.
Handling needles, vials and skin in a way that keeps germs out of the product and the injection site.
Aspartate aminotransferase, an enzyme found mainly in the liver and muscle. Blood levels are measured as a sign of liver or muscle injury.
Physical weakness or lack of energy.
A long-term lung condition in which the airways narrow and swell, causing wheezing, coughing and shortness of breath.
Adenosine triphosphate, the molecule cells use to store and carry energy.
An irregular, often rapid heartbeat that starts in the upper chambers of the heart.
A delay or interruption of the electrical signal passing from the upper to the lower chambers of the heart, which can slow the heartbeat.
A developmental condition that affects communication, social interaction and behavior.
A molecule made by the body itself that the immune system mistakenly treats as foreign and attacks.
A condition in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own healthy tissues.
A pre-filled, spring-loaded device that gives an injection at the push of a button.
A condition in which there are no sperm in the semen.
Sterile water containing a preservative, usually benzyl alcohol, that stops bacteria from growing. It is used to dissolve powdered drugs.
A rare inherited disorder that can cause obesity, vision loss, extra fingers or toes and kidney problems.
A rare inherited disorder, mostly in boys, that affects heart muscle, muscle strength, white blood cells and growth.
Long-acting insulin that supplies a steady background level between meals and overnight.
The starting measurement taken before treatment begins, used as the point of comparison for later results.
Brain-derived neurotrophic factor, a protein that supports the survival, growth and connections of nerve cells.
An inherited condition that causes progressive muscle weakness, milder and slower than Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
A noncancerous enlargement of the prostate gland that can cause trouble urinating.
A class of sedative drugs used for anxiety, seizures and sleep problems. They slow brain activity and can cause dependence.
A preservative added to some injectable liquids, including bacteriostatic water, to prevent bacterial growth.
A receptor on fat and bladder muscle cells that responds to adrenaline-like signals, helping trigger fat breakdown and heat production.
The date after which a compounded or reconstituted medicine should no longer be used, set by how long it stays stable and sterile.
Relating to bile, the liver, the bile ducts and the gallbladder.
A thick mix of bile particles and cholesterol crystals in the gallbladder that can develop into gallstones.
A protein in the blood that attaches to a hormone and carries it, controlling how much is free to act.
The fraction of a dose that reaches the bloodstream in active form.
Safe to use in contact with living tissue without causing harmful reactions.
A layer of bacteria that sticks to a surface and is protected by a slimy coating.
A measurable substance or sign in blood, other fluids or tissue that shows a normal or abnormal process or a response to treatment.
A short peptide marketed as helping regulate gene activity in specific tissues. The claim is largely unproven in human trials.
Describes a study in which participants, researchers or both do not know who gets the active treatment and who gets placebo.
The amount of calcium in the blood, tightly controlled by the body and checked with a blood test.
Clumps of blood that form when platelets and proteins stick together, which can block a blood vessel.
Measurements of the number of red cells, white cells and platelets in a blood sample.
Fats carried in the blood, mainly cholesterol and triglycerides, also called lipids.
The amount of glucose in the blood, the body's main source of energy.
Medicines that prevent blood clots from forming or growing, such as warfarin or apixaban.
A tightly packed layer of cells lining brain blood vessels that blocks many substances from entering the brain.
The proportion of the body made up of fat, muscle, bone and water.
A number calculated from weight and height, used to screen for underweight, overweight and obesity.
Losing fat and gaining muscle at the same time, so body weight may change little.
A single dose given all at once, as opposed to a slow or continuous delivery.
A measure of the amount of mineral in bone, used to judge bone strength and fracture risk.
The process by which cells break down old bone and release its minerals into the blood.
Blood or urine substances that show how fast bone is being broken down and rebuilt.
Surgery that removes a section of the intestine.
The strongest warning the FDA requires on a drug label, highlighting serious or life-threatening risks.
A slower than normal heart rate, usually below 60 beats per minute.
An FDA designation that speeds development and review of a drug for a serious condition when early evidence shows a major improvement over existing treatment.
Given or absorbed through the inside of the cheek.
Active ingredients in raw form, before they are made into a finished medicine. Compounders use them to prepare custom drugs.
Given directly into a vein through a needle or tube, also called intravenous.
Tumors of the thyroid C cells, which make calcitonin. Some GLP-1 drugs carry a boxed warning about them after rodent studies.
A receptor on cell surfaces that responds to hepatocyte growth factor and helps drive cell growth, movement and tissue repair.
A protein made by the liver when there is inflammation. Blood levels are used as a marker of inflammation.
A buildup of calcium deposits in body tissue.
Receptors that respond to calcitonin, a hormone that helps lower blood calcium and slows bone breakdown.
A thin, hollow tube inserted into the body to deliver or remove fluid.
The ability of a substance to cause cancer, often tested in animal studies.
Slow-growing tumors that usually start in the digestive tract or lungs and can release hormone-like substances.
Cancer that begins in the skin or in tissue that lines or covers internal organs.
An abnormal heart rhythm, where the heart beats too fast, too slow or unevenly.
The amount of blood the heart pumps out per minute.
A fat molecule found in the inner membrane of mitochondria that is needed for cell energy production.
A disease of the heart muscle that makes it enlarged, thickened or stiff and less able to pump blood.
Relating to the heart and blood vessels.
A large study that tests whether a drug changes the rate of heart attacks, strokes or heart-related death.
A substance made in the liver and kidneys that carries fatty acids into cells to be burned for energy.
Numbness, tingling and weakness in the hand caused by pressure on the median nerve at the wrist.
A detailed description of one patient's diagnosis, treatment and outcome.
A report describing outcomes in a group of patients who received similar treatment, with no comparison group.
One of a family of enzymes that carry out programmed cell death.
Describes processes that break down molecules or tissue, such as muscle protein, to release energy.
An FDA list of bulk substances flagged as posing significant safety risks, which may not be used in compounding.
A family of natural proteins made by the immune system that kill bacteria.
Relating to the corpus cavernosum, the sponge-like erectile tissue of the penis that fills with blood during an erection.
A receptor on T cells that receives a second signal needed to fully activate them.
Describes cells that carry the CD34 marker protein on their surface, a feature of blood stem and progenitor cells.
Relating to the cecum, the pouch at the start of the large intestine.
A digestive and immune disease in which eating gluten damages the lining of the small intestine.
The growth of cells in a laboratory dish under controlled conditions, used to study how substances act on cells.
A population of cells grown in the laboratory that can keep dividing, used as a standard model for experiments.
The movement of cells from one place to another, for example into a wound during healing.
A measure of how many cells in a sample are alive and healthy.
A protein on the outer membrane of a cell that binds a signaling molecule and passes the message into the cell.
A spreading bacterial infection of the skin and the tissue beneath it, causing redness, warmth and swelling.
People who have lived to age 100 or older.
The brain and spinal cord.
An eye condition in which fluid builds up under the retina, causing blurred or distorted vision.
Relating to the cerebellum, the part of the brain that helps control balance and coordination.
A blockage of an artery supplying the brain, which can cause a stroke.
Relating to the blood vessels of the brain and the blood flow through them.
Reduced blood flow to the brain, which can cause dizziness, confusion or temporary stroke-like symptoms.
A document from a laboratory or manufacturer reporting the identity, purity and test results of a specific batch of a product.
Light given off by a chemical reaction, used in laboratory tests to detect and measure substances.
A research method that uses engineered receptors and matching drugs to switch specific cells on or off.
Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, the European Medicines Agency committee that reviews drug applications and recommends approval.
Cartilage cells, which make and maintain the cartilage matrix.
A disease affecting the retina and the choroid, the blood-rich layer beneath it, which can impair vision.
The combination of DNA and proteins that packs genetic material inside the cell nucleus.
A long-lasting condition marked by deep tiredness that does not improve with rest, often with trouble concentrating and unrefreshing sleep.
Long-term liver inflammation caused by infection with the hepatitis B virus that lasts more than 6 months.
Long-term liver inflammation caused by infection with the hepatitis C virus.
A proposed condition in which long-lasting inflammation is thought to follow exposure to mold or other biotoxins. It is not widely accepted as a diagnosis.
An animal research model in which repeated low-level stressors are used to produce depression-like behavior.
Clinician's Interview-Based Impression of Change Plus, a rating in which a clinician judges overall change in a patient, often used in dementia trials.
The body's roughly 24-hour internal cycle that influences sleep, hormone release and other functions.
A lab procedure that holds blood glucose at a set level with infusions to measure how the body responds to insulin.
A pregnancy confirmed by ultrasound or other clinical signs, rather than by a blood or urine test alone.
An oral drug that blocks estrogen receptors in the brain, raising release of hormones that stimulate ovulation or testosterone production.
The process by which blood thickens into a clot to stop bleeding.
Centimeter, a unit of length equal to one hundredth of a meter.
Continuing medical education, ongoing training that healthcare professionals complete to keep their skills current.
Cytomegalovirus, a common virus that usually causes mild illness but can be serious in people with weak immune systems.
Ciliary neurotrophic factor, a protein that supports the survival and function of nerve cells.
Carbon dioxide, a gas the body produces as waste and breathes out.
Given at the same time as another drug or treatment.
A small non-protein molecule that helps an enzyme carry out its chemical reaction.
A group of people who share a trait or are enrolled together and followed over time in a study.
Inflammation of the colon.
A fibrous protein that gives strength and structure to skin, tendons, bones and other connective tissue.
An exam in which a doctor looks inside the colon using a thin flexible tube with a camera.
A state of deep unconsciousness in which a person cannot be awakened or respond to surroundings.
Having two or more diseases or conditions at the same time.
Participants who finished a study as planned rather than dropping out.
Made by a pharmacy by mixing or preparing ingredients to order, rather than being a mass-produced, FDA-approved product.
A pharmacy that prepares customized medications by combining or altering ingredients for individual orders.
A range of values that likely contains the true effect, given the uncertainty in a study's data.
A condition present from birth in which the brain does not release enough signals to trigger puberty and sex hormone production.
A condition in which a weakened heart cannot pump well enough, allowing fluid to build up in the body.
Tissue that supports, protects and gives structure to other tissues and organs, such as tendon, cartilage and fat.
Delivery of a fluid or drug into a vein steadily over a long period instead of in separate doses.
A condition or circumstance that makes a particular treatment unsafe for a person.
The group in a study that does not receive the treatment being tested, used for comparison.
A drug whose making, possession and use are regulated by law because of its potential for abuse.
A study that compares a treatment group with a control group to see whether the treatment makes a difference.
Sudden, uncontrolled shaking of the body caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain, also called seizures.
Narrowing or blockage of the arteries that supply blood to the heart, usually from plaque buildup.
A temporary structure in the ovary that forms after ovulation and makes progesterone.
Relating to the cortex, the outer layer of an organ, such as the brain or adrenal gland.
Steroid hormones made by the adrenal glands, or drugs that mimic them, that reduce inflammation and suppress immune activity.
A hormone made by the adrenal glands that helps the body respond to stress and regulates blood sugar and inflammation.
Coronavirus disease 2019, a respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus.
A mast cell stabilizer drug that prevents the release of allergy-related chemicals such as histamine.
A chemical bond that joins two molecules or protein strands together, such as those that stiffen collagen.
A trial design in which each participant receives both treatments in turn, so each person serves as their own comparison.
A condition in which one or both testicles have not moved down into the scrotum.
A procedure that scrapes away tissue using a small spoon-shaped instrument.
A condition in which abnormal protein deposits build up in the skin, often causing itchy patches.
Deposits of calcium in the skin, which form hard lumps or patches.
An enzyme that forms a ring-shaped molecule, such as adenylyl cyclase making the signaling molecule cAMP.
A drug that suppresses the immune system, used to prevent organ transplant rejection and treat some immune conditions.
A liver enzyme that breaks down many drugs, so changes in its activity can alter drug levels.
A drug or substance that slows the CYP3A4 enzyme, which can raise blood levels of drugs it breaks down.
An inherited disease that causes thick, sticky mucus, mainly harming the lungs and digestive system.
Inflammation of the bladder lining, often from infection.
An exam of the bladder and urethra using a thin tube with a light and camera.
A small protein released by immune and other cells that signals to and influences immune activity.
Protecting cells from damage.
A mirror-image form of an amino acid, rarely found in natural proteins, sometimes used in peptides to resist breakdown.
A blood test marker of clot breakdown, used to help check for abnormal blood clots.
A mathematical method that works backward from hormone blood levels to estimate when and how much was released.
The deepest stage of non-REM sleep, marked by slow brain waves, also called slow-wave sleep.
The rounded shoulder muscle, a common site for injections.
Immune cells that capture foreign material and show it to other immune cells to start an immune response.
A state where the body has adapted to a drug, so stopping it can cause withdrawal symptoms.
A feeling of being detached from your own body, thoughts or feelings, as if watching yourself from outside.
Inflammation of the skin, often causing redness, itching or rash.
A simple sugar (glucose) used in water-based solutions given by injection or drip.
Dihydrotestosterone, a potent hormone made from testosterone in the prostate, skin and other tissues.
The medical name for diabetes, a disease in which blood sugar stays too high because the body makes too little insulin or cannot use it well.
Open sores on the feet of people with diabetes, often slow to heal because of poor circulation and nerve damage.
Swelling in the central part of the retina caused by leaking blood vessels in people with diabetes, which can blur vision.
Damage to the blood vessels of the retina at the back of the eye caused by diabetes.
A test used to find out what disease or condition a person has.
A treatment that filters waste and extra fluid from the blood when the kidneys can no longer do it.
The lower number in a blood pressure reading, measuring pressure in the arteries between heartbeats.
Obesity produced in lab animals by feeding a high-fat or high-calorie diet, used to test weight-loss drugs.
A product taken by mouth that contains vitamins, minerals, herbs or other ingredients meant to add to the diet.
A heart muscle disease in which the heart chambers stretch and weaken, so the heart pumps blood less well.
The liquid used to dissolve or dilute a powdered drug before use.
A molecule made of two linked nucleotides, such as nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+).
A molecule made of two amino acids joined together.
Stopping a treatment, either planned or because of side effects or other reasons.
A serious condition in which clotting is switched on throughout the body, forming small clots and causing bleeding.
Swelling or stretching of a hollow organ, most often a bloated abdomen.
The time it takes for a drug level in the blood to fall by half as the drug spreads from blood into body tissues.
Dimethyl sulfoxide, a solvent used to dissolve compounds for lab and some topical use.
Deoxyribonucleic acid, the molecule in cells that carries genetic instructions.
The largest ovarian follicle in a cycle, the one most likely to release an egg.
A brain chemical that carries signals between nerve cells and plays a role in movement, motivation and reward.
The share of dopamine transporters, proteins that clear dopamine from nerve junctions, that are blocked by a drug.
Using drugs or other substances to improve athletic performance, usually banned in sport.
Raising the dose step by step, either to improve tolerance or in trials to find the highest safe dose.
Adjusting a dose gradually up or down to reach the wanted effect.
Describes an effect that gets stronger or weaker as the dose changes.
A side effect serious enough in a trial to stop further dose increases.
A study design that tests several doses to find which ones work best and are tolerated.
The relationship between the size of a dose and the size of the effect it produces.
A study design in which neither participants nor researchers know who gets the active treatment.
A participant who leaves a study before it ends.
A chemical addition that lets a peptide attach to proteins in the blood so that it lasts much longer in the body.
A condition in which the eyes do not make enough tears or the tears evaporate too fast, causing irritation.
Dextran sulfate sodium, a chemical added to mouse drinking water to cause colitis in lab studies.
A drug that activates two different receptors at once, such as the GLP-1 and GIP receptors.
An inherited disease that causes progressive muscle weakness and wasting, mostly in boys.
An abnormal and often unpleasant sensation, such as burning or tingling, from a normal touch.
Upset stomach, with symptoms such as discomfort, fullness or indigestion.
Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing.
Poor control of a body process, so it works too much, too little or at the wrong time.
A segment at the end of the IGF-1 precursor protein that is cut off when mature IGF-1 forms.
Half maximal effective concentration, the concentration of a drug that produces half of its maximum effect.
Electrocardiogram, a recording of the heart's electrical activity over time.
Erectile dysfunction, trouble getting or keeping an erection firm enough for sex.
Swelling caused by excess fluid trapped in body tissues.
Electroencephalogram, a recording of electrical activity in the brain.
How well a treatment produces the intended benefit under study conditions.
Estimated glomerular filtration rate, a blood test based estimate of how well the kidneys filter waste.
The final stage of development of an egg in the ovary before it can be released and fertilized.
The percentage of blood the heart pumps out with each beat, a measure of heart function.
A stretchy protein in skin, blood vessels and lungs that lets tissues return to their shape.
A mineral such as sodium, potassium or calcium that carries an electric charge in body fluids.
Blood levels of minerals such as sodium or potassium that are too high or too low.
The actual amount of calcium in a supplement, as opposed to the total weight of the calcium compound.
A raised maze with open and enclosed arms used to measure anxiety-like behavior in rodents.
The time it takes for the amount of a drug in the body to fall by half as the body clears it.
European Medicines Agency, the body that evaluates and approves medicines in the European Union.
A fertility treatment step in which an embryo made in a lab is placed into the uterus.
A US FDA pathway that allows an unapproved medical product to be used during a public health emergency.
A disorder of brain function caused by disease, injury, drugs or toxins.
Complete or near complete kidney failure that needs dialysis or a kidney transplant.
Relating to glands that release hormones into the bloodstream.
Made inside the body, rather than taken from outside.
The cells that line the inside of blood vessels.
A toxin from the cell wall of certain bacteria that can trigger fever and inflammation if it contaminates a product.
An outcome a trial measures to judge whether a treatment works.
The number of calories the body burns, including at rest and during activity.
A diet that supplies fewer calories than the body uses.
A small natural peptide in the brain and body that acts on opioid receptors to reduce pain.
An enzyme that breaks down enkephalins.
The ability to get all needed nutrition by mouth or tube feeding without intravenous nutrition.
Cells lining the gut that release hormones in response to food.
A protein that speeds up chemical reactions in the body.
A signaling protein that attracts eosinophils, a type of immune cell involved in allergy.
The end part of a long bone, separated from the shaft by a growth plate in children.
Nosebleed.
Erythropoietic protoporphyria, an inherited disorder that makes skin painfully sensitive to light.
Trouble getting or keeping an erection firm enough for sex.
Extracellular signal-regulated kinase, an enzyme in a signaling pathway that controls cell growth and division.
A published correction to an error in a journal article.
Estrogen-related receptors, proteins that help regulate how cells make energy.
Redness of the skin.
An inherited disorder that makes skin painfully sensitive to light.
A hormone made mainly by the kidneys that tells the bone marrow to make red blood cells.
A precise statement of what a trial aims to measure, including the population, the outcome and how events like stopping treatment are handled.
The main form of estrogen, a sex hormone.
The fertile phase of the reproductive cycle in female animals.
Using hormones to bring a group of female animals into estrus at the same time.
The dark brown to black pigment that gives skin and hair their color.
An intense feeling of happiness or well-being.
Having enough complete data to be included in a study's analysis, as in evaluable participants.
A dosing schedule in which a dose is taken once, skipped for a day, then taken again on the following day.
A family of peptides first found in Gila monster saliva. Some, such as exendin-4, act on the GLP-1 receptor.
A compound that triggers some of the same cell responses as physical exercise, such as improved energy use in muscle.
Coming from outside the body, such as a hormone given as a medicine rather than made by the body itself.
A way for a patient who cannot join a clinical trial to receive an investigational therapy outside the trial.
A notice from a journal warning readers that a published paper may have problems, issued before a final decision such as a retraction.
A follow-on study that keeps treating or tracking participants after the main trial ends to gather longer-term data.
An FDA process that speeds up development and review of drugs for serious conditions with unmet medical needs.
Blood sugar level measured after not eating for several hours, usually overnight.
Poor absorption of dietary fat from the gut, which can cause loose, greasy stools.
The total weight of body fat, as opposed to muscle, bone and other tissue.
The release of stored fat from fat cells into the blood so it can be used for energy.
The burning of fat by the body's cells to produce energy.
Everything in the body that is not fat, including muscle, bone, organs and water.
A chain of carbon atoms attached to a drug to help it stay in the blood longer.
A condition in which excess fat builds up in the liver.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, the agency that reviews and regulates drugs, devices and food.
The official FDA-approved information sheet for a drug, listing its approved uses, directions and safety warnings.
Reviewed and cleared by the FDA for a specific use, based on evidence of safety and effectiveness.
A loop in which a hormone or its effects signal the body to make less of that same hormone.
The narrow part of the thigh bone just below the ball of the hip joint, often measured in bone density scans.
Forced expiratory volume in one second, the amount of air a person can forcefully blow out in the first second. A common lung function measure.
Cells in connective tissue that make collagen and help heal wounds.
The growth of excess scar-like fibrous tissue in an organ.
The first study in which a new drug is given to people after earlier lab and animal testing.
One product that contains two or more drugs in set amounts.
Extra fluid held in the body's tissues, often causing swelling in the legs, hands or face.
Sudden redness and warmth of the face or upper body caused by widened blood vessels.
Darkening of the skin in a small, localized patch.
A pituitary hormone that helps eggs mature in the ovaries and supports sperm production in the testes.
The period after treatment or enrollment during which participants' health is monitored.
A list of drugs covered by a health plan or stocked by a hospital or pharmacy.
A protein that switches genes on and off and helps control glucose and fat metabolism.
A protein that switches genes on and off and helps keep aged cells from dying.
Formyl peptide receptor-like 1, an immune cell receptor involved in inflammation signaling.
Bone breaks caused by a minor fall or stress that would not normally break a healthy bone.
Dried by freezing and removing water under vacuum, leaving a powder that is mixed with liquid before use.
Repeated freezing and thawing of a sample or solution, which can break down some compounds.
The outer layer of the front part of the brain, involved in planning, decisions and movement.
A group of brain disorders caused by loss of nerve cells in the front and side parts of the brain, affecting behavior and language.
Loss of menstrual periods caused by the brain reducing reproductive hormone signals due to stress, low weight or heavy exercise.
A peptide joined to another molecule or protein to form one combined compound.
A study finding that a treatment is unlikely to show benefit, which can lead to stopping the trial early.
Gram, a unit of mass equal to one thousandth of a kilogram.
Gamma-aminobutyric acid, the brain's main calming chemical messenger that reduces nerve cell activity.
A receptor on nerve cells that GABA activates, reducing nerve activity and producing calming effects.
A small pear-shaped organ under the liver that stores bile, a fluid that helps digest fat.
Problems of the gallbladder such as gallstones or inflammation.
Hard lumps that form in the gallbladder from bile and can block bile flow and cause pain.
The speed at which food leaves the stomach and moves into the small intestine.
A hormone released by the stomach after eating that triggers stomach acid release.
Relating to the digestive tract, including the stomach and intestines.
